task.goal: Help adults in a community workshop compare the total cost of two household energy plans with different fixed and usage charges.
hard_constraints: One facilitator has 50 minutes, calculators, paper and no live pricing access.
Use fictional prices and avoid recommending a real provider.
Mixed numeracy levels must have a meaningful participation route; assess a new usage scenario individually, including a crossover case.
task.available_resources: Printed fictional bills and rate cards.
task.expected_result: A practical comparison activity and individual decision check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Build and compare complete fictional bills
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Participants construct each bill by adding its fixed charge to its usage charge. Fictional monthly Plan A costs $12 plus $0.20 per kWh; Plan B costs $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. State that both cover the same service, with no taxes, discounts or other charges. The mechanism is making both cost components visible: comparing usage rates alone can produce the wrong decision.

Use 5 minutes to introduce the task, 10 to model a 40 kWh bill, 15 for pairs to calculate and compare bills at 60 and 200 kWh, 8 to discuss when the cheaper plan changes, 10 for an individual check and 2 for collection. Provide printed bill templates with separate fixed-charge, usage-charge and total boxes. Participants can use calculators, write calculations or place preprinted component amounts into the boxes. Partners alternate calculating and explaining; choosing and explaining a component gives less confident participants a substantive role.

The individual check introduces 100, 120 and 140 kWh. Each person records both totals and chooses A, B or equal at each usage. Expected totals are $32/$34, $36/$36 and $40/$38. Ask why the preferred plan changes. This directly assesses the crossover rather than merely asking for its definition.

Preparation requires fictional rate cards, component strips, templates and an answer key. The approach assumes participants can connect a stated usage amount to a calculator multiplication. Its main limitation is that repeated arithmetic may obscure the broader relationship unless discussion explicitly connects the cases.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before wider use, compare the template with an ordinary rate-card-only worksheet using matched practice questions. Then give everyone the same individual check. Inspect whether participants include fixed charges, identify equality at 120 kWh and select opposite plans on either side. The proposed advantage is unsupported if templates yield no clearer component explanations or fewer fixed-charge omissions than the plain worksheet.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Find the crossing on a cost map
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Participants compare two plotted cost lines, using their intersection to divide usage into regions where each plan costs less. Use fictional Plan A at $12 monthly plus $0.20 per kWh and Plan B at $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. Assume identical service and no additional charges. The outcome changes at 120 kWh because A starts lower but rises faster.

Allocate 5 minutes to the scenario and graph axes, 10 to calculating and plotting a worked point, 15 to pairs completing a printed graph, 8 to interpreting its crossing, 10 to an individual check and 2 to collection. Print a large, clearly labelled grid covering 0–240 kWh and $0–$64. Supply a value table at 0, 60, 180 and 240 kWh, with some totals completed and others left for calculator work. Participants draw each straight line and mark which is lower in different regions. Distinguish lines with letters and solid/dashed styles rather than colour alone.

Mixed-numeracy roles include calculating missing values, locating supplied coordinates and explaining which line is lower. Everyone must make at least one comparison. Model axis reading explicitly; graph familiarity cannot be assumed.

For the individual check, use previously unpractised usage values of 100, 120 and 140 kWh. Each participant marks them, selects the cheaper plan or equality, and verifies the 120 kWh result numerically. Accept graph estimates for other totals while requiring correct decisions.

Preparation needs printed grids, tables, rate cards and an answer key. The visual mechanism makes the changing preference visible, but inaccurate plotting or inaccessible print can defeat it; exact equality needs arithmetic confirmation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the graph activity with a simple completed cost table using the same prices and time allowance. Use the same unseen individual scenarios afterward. Inspect decision accuracy, recognition of equality and axis-reading errors. If participants who struggled with arithmetic also struggle to read the graph, or graph estimates reverse near-crossing decisions, the proposed accessibility benefit has failed and the graph needs revision.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repay the higher fixed charge through usage savings
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Participants track whether usage savings repay an extra fixed charge. Fictional Plan A costs $12 monthly plus $0.20 per kWh; Plan B costs $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. B therefore begins $12 behind but saves $0.10 for every kWh used. At 120 kWh the savings exactly cover the extra fixed charge. Below that usage A is cheaper; above it B is cheaper. Assume equal service and no other charges.

Spend 5 minutes establishing the fictional scenario, 10 modelling the extra-charge comparison, 15 on paired paper tracking, 8 linking it to complete bills, 10 on an individual check and 2 collecting responses. Print a $12 'extra fixed cost' strip divided into twelve $1 boxes. Each 10 kWh of usage earns B $1 in savings, so participants mark boxes to represent savings and compare the amount earned with the $12 hurdle. Use 40, 80 and 200 kWh during practice. Explain that the boxes represent differences between bills, not either bill's total.

Participants may calculate savings, mark boxes or explain whether the hurdle has been reached. Include one worked example with complete bills to establish why this shortcut is valid. The facilitator checks that participants can explain what each dollar represents.

Individually, participants assess new usage values of 100, 120 and 140 kWh, recording B's usage savings, the cheaper plan or equality, and the dollar difference. Expected savings are $10, $12 and $14, producing A cheaper by $2, equality and B cheaper by $2. They also calculate both full bills for one scenario.

Preparation requires rate cards, printed strips, practice sheets and an answer key. This mechanism reduces repeated arithmetic, but assumes constant usage rates; tiered prices or extra fees require a different comparison.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the savings-strip method with ordinary full-bill calculation on matched practice cases, followed by the same individual check. Inspect whether participants correctly distinguish savings from total cost and correctly handle the crossover. The shortcut fails its smallest useful test if learners select plans correctly but cannot reconcile one decision with the complete bills, indicating an unexplained rule rather than transferable understanding.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Audit misleading energy-plan advice
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Participants act as consumer-advice reviewers: find what a fictional recommendation overlooks, produce a counterexample, and rewrite it accurately. The main mechanism is correcting plausible mistakes and testing claims, which could help adults recognize when an attractive rate does not imply a lower total bill.

Use fictional monthly Plan A at $12 plus $0.20 per kWh and Plan B at $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. Assume identical service, constant rates and no other charges. Print these assumptions on every rate card.

Allocate 6 minutes to reading the cards, 8 to modelling an audit, 15 to paired reviews, 9 to discussing corrected advice, 10 to an individual check and 2 to collection. Model the claim, ‘A always costs $12,’ using a completed 60 kWh bill to expose the missing usage charge. Pairs then audit ‘B is always cheaper because its usage rate is lower’ and ‘A is always cheaper because its fixed charge is lower.’ Provide completed fictional bills at 30 and 210 kWh, with separate charge components. Participants identify evidence that defeats each claim and replace ‘always’ with a conditional explanation.

For mixed numeracy, participants may calculate independently or use supplied component totals to circle contradictory evidence and explain it verbally. Each partner must contribute a correction; arithmetic speed does not determine participation.

Individually, everyone receives new scenarios at 100, 120 and 140 kWh. They record both totals, choose A, B or equal, and correct an overgeneralized recommendation. An optional component table supports calculation without naming the winner. The answer key gives $32/$34, $36/$36 and $40/$38.

Preparation requires rate cards, fictional advice slips, bills and an answer key. Reading demands and memorized corrections are limitations; the individual cases check whether learners can transfer the principle.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot the audit activity against a straightforward worked-example-and-practice worksheet using the same rates, time and individual check. Inspect fixed-charge omissions, crossover decisions and explanations. The proposed benefit is unsupported if participants can reject rehearsed claims but perform no better on the new cases, particularly equality at 120 kWh.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Compare plans through a fixed-budget challenge
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Participants ask how much energy the same household budget buys under each plan, then connect that result to total bills. This reverses the usual calculation: subtract the fixed charge from a budget, then divide what remains by the usage rate. The mechanism makes the fixed charge visible as money unavailable for buying energy, while showing when a lower usage rate compensates for it.

Use fictional monthly Plan A at $12 plus $0.20 per kWh and Plan B at $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. Assume identical service, constant rates, divisible usage and no additional charges. Explain that the budgets are comparison tools, not advice about adequate household consumption.

Allocate 5 minutes to the scenario, 10 to modelling, 15 to paired budget challenges, 8 to connecting budgets with bills, 10 to an individual check and 2 to collection. Model a $30 budget: after fixed charges, A buys 90 kWh and B buys 60 kWh. Pairs investigate $28, $36 and $44 budgets. At $36 both buy 120 kWh; above that budget B buys more. Verify one result by rebuilding its complete bill.

Provide paper mats with budget, fixed charge, money remaining and affordable usage boxes. Participants can calculate or use supplied intermediate amounts to explain which plan buys more energy. Partners alternate explaining and checking. This provides substantive participation without requiring everyone to perform division unaided.

Individually, participants calculate both bills for previously unused demands of 100, 120 and 140 kWh and choose A, equal or B. Expected totals are $32/$34, $36/$36 and $40/$38. Ask how the equal-budget activity explains the middle result.

Preparation requires printed rate cards, mats, support tables and an answer key. The approach requires explicit support for division and may confuse affordability with actual consumption; its accessibility advantage is uncertain.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In a small pilot, give one group the budget challenge and another ordinary complete-bill practice, with equal time and identical individual checks. Inspect both total-cost accuracy and whether learners explain the 120 kWh equality. Include one question distinguishing affordable usage from actual usage. Reject the proposed advantage if the budget group makes more reversed plan choices or treats budget capacity as the household’s consumption, even if it completes the practice mats correctly.

EXPAND.title: Audit competing claims before choosing a plan
EXPAND.proposal:
Participants learn by diagnosing plausible mistakes in fictional bill comparisons, then repairing the reasoning. The mechanism is error discrimination: distinguishing a convincing claim from a valid total-cost comparison. What changes the outcome is whether participants check both the fixed charge and the usage charge instead of trusting a low advertised rate or a confident calculation.

Use fictional monthly Plan A at $12 plus $0.20 per kWh and Plan B at $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. Assume identical service, constant rates and no taxes, discounts or additional charges. Print these assumptions on every rate card.

Allocate 6 minutes to introducing the prices and modelling calculator entry, 8 to auditing one worked claim, 16 to paired audits, 8 to discussing repairs, 10 to an individual check and 2 to collection. Model the incorrect claim that B must always be cheaper because its usage rate is lower. At 50 kWh, complete totals of $22 and $29 refute it.

Pairs receive three fictional customer claims at 80, 160 and 200 kWh: one omits a fixed charge, one contains a multiplication error, and one is correct. Provide calculations beside each claim. Participants label each step as supported or needing repair, correct it and explain the resulting choice. Partners alternate checking and explaining. Less confident participants can match printed charge labels to calculation steps and identify missing components; calculators support repairs without requiring mental arithmetic.

Individually, everyone evaluates previously unused scenarios of 100, 120 and 140 kWh, recording both totals and choosing A, equal or B. Expected totals are $32/$34, $36/$36 and $40/$38. Ask for one sentence explaining why a single plan does not win throughout.

Preparation requires rate cards, audit sheets, charge labels and an answer key. Reading demands and accidentally remembering incorrect examples are limitations; clearly mark and collect corrected versions. The accessibility benefit remains uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment: Pilot against a simple worksheet that supplies correct worked examples with the same prices and practice usages, allowing equal time. Give both groups the same individual check. Inspect fixed-charge omissions, total accuracy, recognition of the crossover and explanations. The proposed mechanism is not supported if auditing produces no improvement over correct examples, or if participants repeat the planted errors on the new scenarios. With a small workshop, treat this as a practical revision check rather than evidence of general effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Predict, test, and revise a personal decision rule
EXPAND.proposal:
Participants first commit to a prediction, then use calculated bills to test and revise their own rule for choosing a plan. The mechanism is prediction followed by feedback: a discrepancy between an expected winner and the actual totals gives participants a reason to reconsider which charges matter. Unlike auditing supplied mistakes, the activity works with participants’ own expectations. Whether this improves understanding beyond straightforward calculation is uncertain.

Use fictional monthly Plan A at $12 plus $0.20 per kWh and Plan B at $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. Assume identical service, constant rates, and no other charges. Print these assumptions beside the prices.

Allocate 5 minutes to introducing the cards, 5 to private predictions, 8 to modelling calculator entry, 14 to paired testing, 6 to revising rules, 10 to an individual check, and 2 to collection. Before calculating, everyone predicts A, B, equal, or unsure at 40, 80, and 200 kWh and records a short reason. Pairs then calculate both totals and compare their results with their predictions. Each person completes a prompt: ‘I expected __; the totals showed __; my rule now is __.’ Correct initial predictions can be strengthened by explaining why they held.

Support mixed numeracy with labelled calculation boxes, calculator keystroke examples, and paper choices participants can circle. Participants may draw or write their explanation; partners alternate entering calculations and interpreting results. Predictions remain private to reduce embarrassment.

Individually, participants assess new usages of 100, 120, and 140 kWh, recording both totals and choosing A, equal, or B. The answer key gives $32/$34, $36/$36, and $40/$38. Require a brief explanation of why the choice changes.

Preparation requires printed rate cards, prediction and calculation sheets, and an answer key. The approach assumes participants will engage with feedback; guessing without examining discrepancies could leave misconceptions unchanged.
EXPAND.experiment: For a small feasibility check within the workshop, give alternating pairs either prediction-first sheets or a simple comparator sheet containing the same calculations without prediction prompts. Keep prices, practice scenarios, support, and time identical. Use the same individual check for everyone. Inspect correct decisions below, at, and above the crossover, plus explanations that connect fixed and usage charges. If prediction-first participants retain their original mistaken rules or complete fewer checks without clearer explanations, that challenges the mechanism’s practical value. A single small workshop cannot establish superiority; use the results to decide whether the extra prediction step merits another trial.

REFINE.title: Candidate 0: carry component support into the individual check
REFINE.proposal:
Original candidate 0 is the strongest fit: constructing complete bills makes both charges visible with familiar paper materials. Its specific weakness is that supported participation during pair work disappears in the individual check, so multiplication difficulty can prevent learners from demonstrating an independent cost comparison.

Keep the complete-bill activity and its 50-minute schedule unchanged: 5 minutes introducing, 10 modelling, 15 practising in pairs, 8 discussing, 10 checking individually and 2 collecting. Change only the individual worksheet: provide an optional printed usage-charge table alongside separate fixed-charge and total boxes. For new scenarios of 100, 120 and 140 kWh, the table supplies A/B usage charges of $20/$10, $24/$12 and $28/$14. Participants independently select the appropriate components, add each plan’s fixed charge, record both totals and choose A, B or equal. Everyone completes the same decisions; participants may calculate the usage charges themselves or use the table. This preserves meaningful individual assessment without making multiplication fluency the gatekeeper.

Prerequisites are fictional monthly rate cards—A: $12 plus $0.20/kWh; B: $24 plus $0.10/kWh—bill templates, the optional table and an answer key. State identical service, constant rates and no other charges. Expected totals are $32/$34, $36/$36 and $40/$38. Ask participants to complete: ‘Below 120 kWh ___ costs less; at 120 ___; above 120 ___.’ Remaining limit: using supplied subtotals demonstrates component selection, addition and comparison, but does not establish independent multiplication skill.
REFINE.experiment: Prototype the revised individual sheet with adults who need the component support during practice. Give the three new scenarios without partner assistance; the facilitator may read instructions aloud without identifying components or winners. Check whether participants select the correct usage charges, include fixed charges and identify A/equal/B across the crossover. The repair fails its smallest useful check if supported participants still cannot complete the comparison independently, or mistake supplied usage charges for total bills. Record table use so successful comparisons are not reported as evidence of unaided multiplication.

Preparation needs printed grids, tables, rate cards and an answer key. The visual mechanism makes the changing preference visible, but inaccurate plotting or inaccessible print can defeat it; exact equality needs arithmetic confirmation.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the graph activity with a simple completed cost table using the same prices and time allowance. Use the same unseen individual scenarios afterward. Inspect decision accuracy, recognition of equality and axis-reading errors. If participants who struggled with arithmetic also struggle to read the graph, or graph estimates reverse near-crossing decisions, the proposed accessibility benefit has failed and the graph needs revision.

SAVE.title: Repay the higher fixed charge through usage savings
SAVE.proposal:
Participants track whether usage savings repay an extra fixed charge. Fictional Plan A costs $12 monthly plus $0.20 per kWh; Plan B costs $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. B therefore begins $12 behind but saves $0.10 for every kWh used. At 120 kWh the savings exactly cover the extra fixed charge. Below that usage A is cheaper; above it B is cheaper. Assume equal service and no other charges.

Spend 5 minutes establishing the fictional scenario, 10 modelling the extra-charge comparison, 15 on paired paper tracking, 8 linking it to complete bills, 10 on an individual check and 2 collecting responses. Print a $12 'extra fixed cost' strip divided into twelve $1 boxes. Each 10 kWh of usage earns B $1 in savings, so participants mark boxes to represent savings and compare the amount earned with the $12 hurdle. Use 40, 80 and 200 kWh during practice. Explain that the boxes represent differences between bills, not either bill's total.

Participants may calculate savings, mark boxes or explain whether the hurdle has been reached. Include one worked example with complete bills to establish why this shortcut is valid. The facilitator checks that participants can explain what each dollar represents.

Individually, participants assess new usage values of 100, 120 and 140 kWh, recording B's usage savings, the cheaper plan or equality, and the dollar difference. Expected savings are $10, $12 and $14, producing A cheaper by $2, equality and B cheaper by $2. They also calculate both full bills for one scenario.

Preparation requires rate cards, printed strips, practice sheets and an answer key. This mechanism reduces repeated arithmetic, but assumes constant usage rates; tiered prices or extra fees require a different comparison.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the savings-strip method with ordinary full-bill calculation on matched practice cases, followed by the same individual check. Inspect whether participants correctly distinguish savings from total cost and correctly handle the crossover. The shortcut fails its smallest useful test if learners select plans correctly but cannot reconcile one decision with the complete bills, indicating an unexplained rule rather than transferable understanding.

SAVE.title: Audit competing claims before choosing a plan
SAVE.proposal:
Participants learn by diagnosing plausible mistakes in fictional bill comparisons, then repairing the reasoning. The mechanism is error discrimination: distinguishing a convincing claim from a valid total-cost comparison. What changes the outcome is whether participants check both the fixed charge and the usage charge instead of trusting a low advertised rate or a confident calculation.

Use fictional monthly Plan A at $12 plus $0.20 per kWh and Plan B at $24 plus $0.10 per kWh. Assume identical service, constant rates and no taxes, discounts or additional charges. Print these assumptions on every rate card.

Allocate 6 minutes to introducing the prices and modelling calculator entry, 8 to auditing one worked claim, 16 to paired audits, 8 to discussing repairs, 10 to an individual check and 2 to collection. Model the incorrect claim that B must always be cheaper because its usage rate is lower. At 50 kWh, complete totals of $22 and $29 refute it.

Pairs receive three fictional customer claims at 80, 160 and 200 kWh: one omits a fixed charge, one contains a multiplication error, and one is correct. Provide calculations beside each claim. Participants label each step as supported or needing repair, correct it and explain the resulting choice. Partners alternate checking and explaining. Less confident participants can match printed charge labels to calculation steps and identify missing components; calculators support repairs without requiring mental arithmetic.

Individually, everyone evaluates previously unused scenarios of 100, 120 and 140 kWh, recording both totals and choosing A, equal or B. Expected totals are $32/$34, $36/$36 and $40/$38. Ask for one sentence explaining why a single plan does not win throughout.

Preparation requires rate cards, audit sheets, charge labels and an answer key. Reading demands and accidentally remembering incorrect examples are limitations; clearly mark and collect corrected versions. The accessibility benefit remains uncertain.
SAVE.experiment: Pilot against a simple worksheet that supplies correct worked examples with the same prices and practice usages, allowing equal time. Give both groups the same individual check. Inspect fixed-charge omissions, total accuracy, recognition of the crossover and explanations. The proposed mechanism is not supported if auditing produces no improvement over correct examples, or if participants repeat the planted errors on the new scenarios. With a small workshop, treat this as a practical revision check rather than evidence of general effectiveness.
